questions.q: For routine urine analysis, the sample the book recommends is:
opts: A random sample taken after vigorous exercise
Urine collected from the urobag of a catheterised patient
The 2nd urine sample of the morning, by midstream technique
questions.exp: The line reads: Sample — 2nd urine sample of morning → midstream technique. The first morning void is not what is printed, and catheterised patients must give fresh urine, never urobag urine. (Book p740)

questions.q: Fill up: Urine must be analysed within ______ hours at room temperature, while the pH should be checked immediately.
questions.exp: Analysis: within 2-4 hours at room temperature (pH to be checked immediately). (Book p740)

questions.q: The preservatives listed for a urine sample are:
questions.exp: Preservation: Formaldehyde, Glutaraldehyde. (Book p740)

questions.q: Up to how long may a urine sample be stored at 2-8°C before analysis?
questions.exp: Storage: 2-8°C upto 12 hours. (Book p740)

questions.q: A marathon runner is scheduled for a routine urine check. To avoid false results from rhabdomyolysis, strenuous physical activity must be avoided for how long before collection?
questions.exp: Strenuous physical activity 72 hrs prior to collection → false results due to rhabdomyolysis. (Book p740)

questions.q: Which statement about urine collection is TRUE?
opts: Strenuous exercise just before collection improves sample quality
pH can reliably be checked after a day at room temperature
Collection during menstruation should be avoided
Urine may be collected from the urobag in catheterised patients
questions.exp: To avoid: strenuous activity 72 hrs prior and collection during menstruation; pH is checked immediately. (Book p740)

questions.q: Fill up: In catheterised patients, urine must always be collected ______ and never from the urobag.
questions.exp: Catheterised patients: always collect fresh urine; do not collect from urobag. (Book p740)

questions.q: The photograph beside the collection instructions, showing gloved hands with a specimen, is captioned:
questions.exp: The photo to the right of the 'Instructions: To Avoid' list carries the caption 'Collection of urine'. (Book p740)

questions.q: In the appearance table, 'pale/white' urine is paired with increased water intake while 'light yellow' is labelled normal.
opts: True — those are the first two rows of the table
False — pale/white marks concentration, light yellow marks dilution
True — and both rows are listed under pathological colours
False — light yellow is paired with increased water intake
questions.exp: Rows 1 and 2 of the APPEARANCE table: Light yellow → Normal; Pale/white → ↑ water intake (the photo beside the table is captioned 'Normal urine colour'). (Book p740)

questions.q: Pink urine on the appearance table is attributed to:
questions.exp: Pink: Desferrioxamine, beetroot. (Book p740)

questions.q: Urine that darkens on long standing points to which drug combination?
questions.exp: Darkening on long standing: Imipenem + cilastatin. (Book p740)

questions.q: Fill up: Green urine in the appearance table is attributed to triamterene, which the page brackets as a ______ blocker.
questions.exp: The row reads 'Green — Triamterene (ENaC blocker)'. (Book p740)

questions.q: Fill up: In the APPEARANCE table, brown urine is attributed to ______.
questions.exp: Row 6 of the table: Brown — Nitrofurantoin. (Book p740)

questions.q: Orange urine in the table is attributed to rifampicin together with:
questions.exp: Orange → Rifampicin, Entacapone (COMT inhibitor). Imipenem + cilastatin is the darkening-on-standing row, nitrofurantoin gives brown, desferrioxamine gives pink. (Book p740)

questions.q: A patient on anti-tuberculosis therapy complains that her urine has turned orange but the dipstick is negative for blood. The table's explanation is:
opts: Rifampicin is a listed cause of orange urine
Bilirubinuria, since orange equals obstructive jaundice
Beetroot ingestion, always a false colour
questions.exp: Rifampicin (with entacapone) is printed under 'Orange' in the colour table; a dipstick negative for blood excludes haematuria as the source of colour. (Book p740)

questions.q: Match each urine colour with its listed cause — 1) Green 2) Brown 3) Orange … A) Nitrofurantoin B) Rifampicin, entacapone C) Triamterene (ENaC blocker)
questions.exp: Green – triamterene (ENaC blocker); brown – nitrofurantoin; orange – rifampicin, entacapone (COMT inhibitor). (Book p740)

questions.q: Which colour-drug pair is NOT as written in the appearance table?
questions.exp: Desferrioxamine gives pink urine; green is triamterene (ENaC blocker). (Book p740)

questions.q: The jar photographed beside the appearance table is captioned:
questions.exp: The photo of a jar of light-yellow urine to the right of the colour table is captioned 'Normal urine colour'; 'High coloured urine' is the p742 photo. (Book p740)

questions.q: A pungent urine odour, unless proven otherwise, signifies infection because bacteria generate:
questions.exp: Pungent: infection (unless proven otherwise) d/t ammonia produced by bacteria. (Book p740)

questions.q: Match each odour with its condition — 1) Musty/mousy 2) Curry/maple syrup 3) Sweaty feet … A) Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) B) Isovaleric acidemia, glutaric aciduria type II C) Phenylketonuria
questions.exp: Musty/mousy – phenylketonuria; curry/maple syrup – MSUD; sweaty feet – isovaleric acidemia, glutaric aciduria type II. (Book p740)

questions.q: A neonate's urine smells of sweaty feet. The differential given is:
opts: Tyrosinemia type 1 or multiple carboxylase deficiency
Isovaleric acidemia or glutaric aciduria type II
questions.exp: Sweaty feet odour: isovaleric acidemia; glutaric aciduria type II. (Book p740)

questions.q: The odour table gives cabbage-like and rancid-butter odour as two separate rows sharing a single condition, tyrosinemia type I.
opts: True — one condition is written across both rows
False — cabbage-like marks tyrosinemia and rancid butter marks hawkinsinuria
False — rancid butter is paired with methyl malonic acidemia
True — and the same condition also explains the fish odour
questions.exp: The table brackets 'Cabbage-like' and 'Rancid butter' against one entry: Tyrosinemia type I. Swimming pool is hawkinsinuria and fish urine is trimethylaminuria. (Book p741)

questions.q: Which odour statement is TRUE as per the table?
opts: Swimming pool odour marks tyrosinemia type 1
Cat urine odour marks multiple carboxylase deficiency
questions.exp: Cat urine – MCD; cabbage-like/rancid butter – tyrosinemia type 1; swimming pool – hawkinsinuria. (Book p741)

questions.q: All of the following odour-disease pairs are as printed EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Acid smell belongs to methyl malonic acidemia; cystinuria gives a sulfurous odour. (Book p741)

questions.q: A mother brings an infant whose urine smells of boiled fish; the child is otherwise well and the dipstick is unremarkable. The table directs you to:
questions.exp: 'Fish urine' is the row for trimethylaminuria; cystinuria is the sulfurous row, PKU the musty/mousy row and MSUD the curry/maple-syrup row. (Book p741)

questions.q: Match each odour with its condition — 1) Fish urine 2) Sulfurous 3) Sweet … A) Beta ketothiolase deficiency B) Trimethylaminuria C) Cystinuria
questions.exp: Fish urine – trimethylaminuria; sulfurous – cystinuria; sweet – beta ketothiolase deficiency. (Book p741)

questions.q: Match each odour in the second half of the table with its condition — 1) Acid smell 2) Sulfurous 3) Sweet … A) Beta ketothiolase deficiency B) Methyl malonic acidemia (MMA) C) Cystinuria D) Multiple carboxylase deficiency
questions.exp: As printed: acid smell → methyl malonic acidemia (MMA), sulfurous → cystinuria, sweet → beta ketothiolase deficiency; the cat-urine odour belongs to multiple carboxylase deficiency. (Book p741)

questions.q: Match each odour with its condition — 1) Cabbage-like / rancid butter 2) Cat urine 3) Swimming pool … A) Hawkinsinuria B) Tyrosinemia type 1 C) Multiple carboxylase deficiency (MCD)
questions.exp: Cabbage-like/rancid butter – tyrosinemia type 1; cat urine – MCD; swimming pool – hawkinsinuria. (Book p741)

questions.q: Fill up: The normal urine pH printed in this table is ______, described as acidic.
questions.exp: Row 1: pH — urine 4–4.5 (Acidic) against blood 7.35–7.40. (Book p741)

questions.q: In the 'Other Properties' table, the specific gravity printed for BLOOD is:
questions.exp: The table pairs urine 1.020–1.040 with blood 1.010; 1.005 is the diabetes-insipidus cut-off in the abnormal-values table below. (Book p741)

questions.q: The normal blood osmolality quoted beside the urine column is:
questions.exp: Blood osmolality 285-290 mOsm/kg against urine 800-900 mOsm/kg. (Book p741)

questions.q: Match each parameter with its normal urine value — 1) pH 2) Specific gravity 3) Osmolality (mOsm/kg) … A) 1.020-1.040 B) 800-900 C) 4-4.5 (acidic)
questions.exp: Urine pH 4-4.5 (acidic); specific gravity 1.020-1.040; osmolality 800-900 mOsm/kg. (Book p741)

questions.q: In the acidification diagram, the cell and luminal pump responsible are:
opts: Alpha-intercalated cells of the cortical collecting duct with H+ ATPase
Principal cells of the cortical collecting duct with Na-K ATPase
Beta-intercalated cells of the proximal tubule with H+ ATPase
Podocytes of the glomerulus with aquaporin-2
questions.exp: Alpha-intercalated cells of cortical collecting duct (CCD) secrete H+ via the luminal H+ ATPase. (Book p741)

questions.q: In the acidification diagram, K+ is drawn entering the α-intercalated cell at the luminal membrane while H+ leaves through the H+ ATPase.
opts: False — K+ is shown leaving the cell into the lumen
False — no potassium arrow appears anywhere in the diagram
True — but the H+ arrow points into the cell, not out
True — the two arrows at the luminal membrane point in opposite directions
questions.exp: The figure labels the luminal membrane H+ ATPase with H+ exiting, a second ATPase with K+ entering, and the boxed cell as the α-intercalated cell of the cortical collecting duct (CCD). (Book p741)

questions.q: Fill up: Secreted H+ buffered by NH3 forms the non-titratable, major acid ______.
questions.exp: NH3 + H+ → NH4+ : non titratable, major acid. (Book p741)

questions.q: Fill up: Buffering of secreted H+ by HPO4 2- yields the titratable acid ______.
questions.exp: HPO4 2- + H+ → H2PO4- : titratable acid. (Book p741)

questions.q: Urinary concentration rests on ADH from the posterior pituitary, the vasa recta and a medullary interstitium whose osmolality is raised by:
questions.exp: Medullary interstitium: ↑ osmolality d/t urea; ADH → free water reabsorption; vasa recta. (Book p741)

questions.q: Urinary concentration on this page is credited to all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: A medullary interstitium whose osmolality is raised by urea
ADH secreted from the posterior pituitary
questions.exp: The three bullets under 'Concentration' are ADH → free water reabsorption, medullary interstitium ↑ osmolality d/t urea, and vasa recta; aldosterone is not listed. (Book p741)

questions.q: A patient's urine pH stays above 5.5 for 3 days while the RFT remains normal. The label for this picture is:
questions.exp: Urine pH > 5.5 for 3 days + normal RFT → Type-1 renal tubular acidosis (RTA). (Book p741)

questions.q: Diabetes insipidus (↑ dilute urine) is flagged in the abnormal-values table when urine specific gravity and urine osmolality fall below:
questions.exp: Rows 2-3 read: urine specific gravity < 1.005; urine osmolality < 200 mOsm/kg → Diabetes insipidus (↑ dilute urine). The earlier bank printed 300; the scan shows 200. (Book p741)

questions.q: A patient with 4 L/day of dilute urine has urine osmolality 150 mOsm/kg and specific gravity 1.003, with a normal serum creatinine. Which row of the abnormal-values table does this match?
opts: Normal concentration, since both values are simply dilute
Diabetes insipidus — specific gravity <1.005 and osmolality <200 mOsm/kg
Isosthenuria — urinary parameters equal to blood parameters
Type-1 RTA — urine pH above 5.5 for 3 days
questions.exp: The table flags diabetes insipidus (↑ dilute urine) when urine specific gravity falls below 1.005 and osmolality below 200 mOsm/kg; isosthenuria instead equals blood parameters and points to ATN/CTID. (Book p741)

questions.q: Isosthenuria, defined as urinary parameters equal to blood parameters, points to:
opts: Prerenal azotemia and bladder outlet obstruction
Acute tubular necrosis and chronic tubulo-interstitial disease
questions.exp: Isosthenuria (urinary parameters = blood parameters): ATN; chronic tubulo-interstitial disease (CTID). (Book p741)

questions.q: High colored urine may present as:
opts: Hematuria with red, pink, tea or cola colored urine
questions.exp: High colored urine can be hematuria, red, pink, tea, cola colored urine. (Book p742)

questions.q: The opening line lists all of these presentations of high-coloured urine EXCEPT:
questions.exp: 'Can be hematuria, red, pink, tea, cola colored urine' — a milky white urine belongs to the pale/white row of the appearance table on p740, not to this line. (Book p742)

questions.q: The photograph of a dark-brown specimen jar at the top right of this page is captioned:
questions.exp: Caption under the jar photo: 'High coloured urine'. (Book p742)

questions.q: The cause-wise split of high colored urine is urological, nephrological and hematological at:
questions.exp: Urological (90%), nephrological (9%), hematological (1%). (Book p742)

questions.q: The commonest urological cause highlighted for high colored urine is:
questions.exp: Urological (90%): carcinoma bladder (m/c). (Book p742)

questions.q: The hematological (1%) category of high colored urine corresponds to:
questions.exp: Hematological (1%): intravascular hemolysis. (Book p742)

questions.q: Of the three branches under 'Causes', the nephrological (9%) branch is the only one left without a named disease on this page.
opts: False — nephrological names glomerulonephritis in brackets
False — the hematological branch also lacks an example
True — and the nephrological share is printed as 1%
True — urological names carcinoma bladder and hematological names intravascular hemolysis
questions.exp: Causes: urological (90%) — carcinoma bladder (m/c); Nephrological (9%) with nothing printed under it; Hematological (1%) — intravascular hemolysis. (Book p742)

questions.q: Fill up: In the approach, a positive dipstick test is followed by the box '______ in urine'.
questions.exp: 1. Dipstick test → Positive → 'Blood in urine' → 2. Centrifugation; the Negative branch lists porphyria and ↑ beetroot intake. (Book p742)

questions.q: A red-tinged urine with a negative dipstick for blood should raise suspicion of:
questions.exp: Dipstick negative: porphyria; ↑ beetroot intake. (Book p742)

questions.q: The centrifugation step of the high-colored-urine approach uses:
questions.exp: Centrifugation of urine at 1600 rpm × 5 minutes. (Book p742)

questions.q: After centrifugation, a clear supernatant tells us that the colour came from:
questions.exp: Clear supernatant → RBC (settles down); high colored supernatant → pigments. (Book p742)

questions.q: All of the following define glomerular hematuria in the flowchart EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Glomerular hematuria: ≥ 40% dysmorphic RBCs / ≥ 5% acanthocytes / single RBC cast + proteinuria. (Book p742)

questions.q: Fill up: Glomerular hematuria criteria include ≥ 40 % dysmorphic RBCs or ≥ ______ % acanthocytes or a single RBC cast with proteinuria.
questions.exp: ≥ 40% dysmorphic RBCs / ≥ 5% acanthocytes / single RBC cast + proteinuria. (Book p742)

questions.q: Fill up: The glomerular-hematuria box requires ≥40% dysmorphic RBCs, ≥5% acanthocytes, or a ______ RBC cast with proteinuria.
questions.exp: Printed criteria: ≥40 % dysmorphic RBCs / ≥5 % acanthocytes / single RBC cast + proteinuria → 3. Biopsy. (Book p742)

questions.q: Once glomerular hematuria is established, the next step in the flowchart is biopsy, which typically reveals:
questions.exp: Biopsy → mesangial disease (IgA nephropathy). (Book p742)

questions.q: The mechanism written for hematuria in IgA nephropathy is:
opts: Mesangial proliferation + matrix expansion → capillary rupture
questions.exp: Mesangial proliferation + matrix expansion → capillary rupture. (Book p742)

questions.q: When the settled RBCs point to a urological cause, the appropriate next step is:
opts: Radiological investigation with USG abdomen and CT
Cystoscopy with biopsy as first step
questions.exp: Urological cause → radiological Ix (USG abdomen, CT). (Book p742)

questions.q: Tea-coloured urine shows blood on dipstick; after centrifugation the supernatant is clear, but microscopy reports 25% dysmorphic RBCs, no casts and no proteinuria. Following the flowchart, the next step is:
opts: Leave the sample undisturbed for 3–6 hours and re-examine the colour
Measure serum complement, because the picture fits nephrological disease
Treat it as a urological cause and send radiological investigation — USG abdomen and CT
Proceed to biopsy, since any dysmorphic cells make it glomerular
questions.exp: The glomerular criteria need ≥40% dysmorphic cells, ≥5% acanthocytes, or a single RBC cast plus proteinuria; none is met, so the left branch runs to 'urological cause → radiological Ix (USG abdomen, CT)'. (Book p742)

questions.q: A still high-colored supernatant is left undisturbed for how long before judging the colour?
questions.exp: Sample undisturbed for 3-6 hours, then observe whether the colour fades or persists. (Book p742)

questions.q: A crushed-limb injury patient passes dark urine; the supernatant colour fades over a few hours. The pigment and its source are:
questions.exp: Colour fades → myoglobin (short t½): rhabdomyolysis. (Book p742)

questions.q: Which statement about the standing-supernatant test is TRUE?
opts: A fading colour implies hemoglobin from hemolysis
The test distinguishes porphyria from beetroot intake
A persistent colour implies hemoglobin with a long half-life from hemolysis
A persistent colour implies myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis
questions.exp: Persistent colour → hemoglobin (long t½): hemolysis; fading → myoglobin (short t½). (Book p742)

questions.q: In the printed approach, which action carries the number 3?
questions.exp: The flowchart is numbered 1. Dipstick test, 2. Centrifugation of urine (1600 rpm × 5 minutes), 3. Biopsy, 4. Sample undisturbed for 3–6 hours — the fourth step sits on the right-hand, high-coloured branch. (Book p742)

questions.sec: Types of RBC & dipstick parameters · p743
questions.q: Which RBC-morphology statement is TRUE as per the figure?
opts: Dysmorphic RBCs belong to the urological category
Crenated and isomorphic RBCs belong to the urological category
Crenated and isomorphic RBCs belong to the nephrological category
questions.exp: Urological: crenated, isomorphic; nephrological: dysmorphic, acanthocytes. (Book p743)

questions.sec: Types of RBC & dipstick parameters · p743
questions.q: In the 'Types of RBC' note, the photographs labelled B and C belong to which category?
questions.exp: Panel A is placed under urological (crenated and isomorphic cells), while panels B and C sit under Nephrological, carrying the dysmorphic cells and the acanthocytes. (Book p743)

questions.sec: Types of RBC & dipstick parameters · p743
questions.q: The nephrological RBCs nicknamed after a famous cartoon mouse are:
questions.exp: Acanthocytes are called Mickey mouse RBCs, seen in the nephrological category. (Book p743)

questions.sec: Types of RBC & dipstick parameters · p743
questions.q: Match each urinary RBC description with its label — 1) Crenated, isomorphic cells 2) Dysmorphic cells 3) Acanthocytes … A) "Mickey mouse" RBCs B) Urological category C) Nephrological category
questions.exp: Urological: crenated, isomorphic; nephrological: dysmorphic; acanthocytes = Mickey mouse RBCs. (Book p743)

questions.sec: Types of RBC & dipstick parameters · p743
questions.q: Which statement about the leukocyte/nitrite dipstick for UTI is TRUE?
opts: It is equally sensitive and specific
It has high specificity but poor sensitivity
It has high sensitivity but poor specificity
questions.exp: Leukocytes + nitrites for urinary tract infections: high specificity, poor sensitivity. (Book p743)

questions.sec: Types of RBC & dipstick parameters · p743
questions.q: The leukocyte and nitrite rows of the dipstick table are printed as two tests sharing one clinical condition, urinary tract infection.
opts: False — nitrites alone carry the UTI entry
False — leukocytes are linked to extravascular hemolysis
True — and the same cell also lists proximal RTA
True — the bracketed line 'high specificity, poor sensitivity' applies to that shared cell
questions.exp: The table merges Leukocytes and Nitrites against 'urinary tract infections (UTI) (High specificity, poor sensitivity)'. (Book p743)

questions.sec: Types of RBC & dipstick parameters · p743
questions.q: A positive urobilinogen pad on the dipstick points to:
questions.exp: Urobilinogen on dipstick: extravascular hemolysis. (Book p743)

questions.sec: Types of RBC & dipstick parameters · p743
questions.q: Euglycemic glycosuria on the dipstick glucose row is the marker of:
questions.exp: Proximal RTA: euglycemic glycosuria. (Book p743)

questions.sec: Types of RBC & dipstick parameters · p743
questions.q: A type-2 diabetic started on an SGLT2 inhibitor shows urine ketones; the glycemic pattern the book pairs with this drug is:
questions.exp: SGLT2 inhibitors: euglycemic ketosis (proximal RTA gives euglycemic glycosuria). (Book p743)

questions.sec: Types of RBC & dipstick parameters · p743
questions.q: Every dipstick row on this page has a clinical condition written against it EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Leukocytes and nitrites share the UTI cell, urobilinogen is matched to extravascular hemolysis and glucose to proximal RTA and SGLT2 inhibitors; the protein, pH, blood, S.G, ketone and conjugated-bilirubin rows are left with a dash. (Book p743)

questions.sec: Types of RBC & dipstick parameters · p743
questions.q: Match each dipstick row with the note printed in its condition cell — 1) Leukocytes and nitrites 2) Urobilinogen 3) Glucose … A) Proximal RTA and SGLT2 inhibitors B) Extravascular hemolysis C) High specificity, poor sensitivity
questions.exp: The merged leukocyte/nitrite cell carries the 'high specificity, poor sensitivity' parenthetical; urobilinogen is paired with extravascular hemolysis; glucose with proximal RTA (euglycemic glycosuria) and SGLT2 inhibitors (euglycemic ketosis). (Book p743)

questions.sec: Types of RBC & dipstick parameters · p743
questions.q: All of the following affect the leukocyte urine dipstick test EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Listed factors: concentrated urine, high relative density, proteinuria, glucosuria, cephalothin & tetracycline, cephalexin, tobramycin. (Book p743)

questions.sec: Types of RBC & dipstick parameters · p743
questions.q: All of the following are listed under 'Factors affecting leukocyte urine dipstick test' EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The left-hand column reads concentrated urine, high relative density, proteinuria and glucosuria; the right-hand column lists cephalothin, tetracycline, cephalexin and tobramycin. (Book p743)

questions.sec: Types of RBC & dipstick parameters · p743
questions.q: Fill up: Cephalothin, tetracycline, cephalexin and tobramycin are listed as drugs affecting the urine ______ dipstick test.
questions.exp: These drugs are listed under factors affecting the leukocyte urine dipstick test. (Book p743)

questions.q: The daily excretion of uromodulin quoted is:
questions.exp: Uromodulin/Tamm Horsfall protein: 70-80 mg/day. (Book p744)

questions.q: Which statement about uromodulin is TRUE?
opts: It is excreted only in glomerular disease
It is the most abundant component of normal urine and forms the matrix of casts
It is the most abundant component of normal plasma
It dissolves cast matrices in alkaline urine
questions.exp: Most abundant component of normal urine; forms matrix of casts. (Book p744)

questions.q: Uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein) is produced by the:
opts: Thick ascending limb of loop of Henle
questions.exp: Produced by thick ascending limb of loop of Henle. (Book p744)

questions.q: Match each urine protein range (mg/day) with its label — 1) <150 2) 150-500 3) >500 … A) Significant proteinuria B) Normal C) Functional proteinuria
questions.exp: <150 normal; 150-500 functional proteinuria; >500 significant proteinuria. (Book p744)

questions.q: An anxious student presents before exams with urine protein of 300 mg/day. The book's category for this level is:
questions.exp: 150-500 mg/day: functional proteinuria (stress, anxiety, menses, protein supplements). (Book p744)

questions.q: Each of these is listed against 'functional proteinuria' in the levels table EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The 150–500 mg/day row reads: Functional proteinuria — stress, anxiety, menses, protein supplements; fever is not printed there (it belongs to the febrile proteinuria teaching elsewhere). (Book p744)

questions.q: Fill up: Significant proteinuria in a non-pregnant adult is urine protein above ______ mg/day.
questions.exp: >500 mg/day: significant proteinuria. (Book p744)

questions.q: Fill up: In pregnancy, significant proteinuria is defined as urine protein greater than ______ mg/day.
questions.exp: >300 mg/day: significant proteinuria in pregnancy (vs >500 otherwise). (Book p744)

questions.q: The injury chain written for albuminuria runs: albumin → tubular injury → inflammation → ______ → fibrosis.
questions.exp: Albumin → tubular injury → inflammation → TGF-β → fibrosis. (Book p744)

questions.q: The flow of injury printed on this page runs albumin → tubular injury → inflammation → TGF-β → fibrosis.
opts: False — TGF-β precedes tubular injury in the printed order
True — but the chain starts with protein, not albumin
True — fibrosis is the terminal arrow of the chain
False — the chain ends at inflammation
questions.exp: 'Albumin levels' section: Albumin → Tubular injury → Inflammation → TGF-β → Fibrosis; this is why even moderately elevated albumin requires further evaluation. (Book p744)

questions.q: Microalbuminuria (moderately elevated albumin) spans urinary albumin of:
questions.exp: <30 normal; 30-300 microalbuminuria; >300 albuminuria. (Book p744)

questions.q: A 24-hour urinary albumin of 450 mg falls into which row of the albumin table?
questions.exp: Urinary albumin rows: <30 normal, 30–300 microalbuminuria (moderately elevated albumin in urine), >300 albuminuria. The 150–500 band is the total-protein table, not the albumin table. (Book p744)

questions.q: Moderately elevated urine albumin matters because it is a:
opts: Benign finding that needs no further evaluation
Marker of vascular integrity with higher thrombosis (CVA, CAD) risk from endothelial injury
Marker of isolated lower urinary tract infection
questions.exp: Marker of vascular integrity; ↑ risk of thrombosis (CVA, CAD) d/t endothelial injury; requires further evaluation. (Book p744)

questions.q: Match each numbered test with what it measures — 1) Test 1 2) Test 2 3) Test 3 … A) Spot urine albumin–creatinine ratio B) Spot urine protein–creatinine ratio C) 24 hour urine protein D) Qualitative dipstick reading
questions.exp: The list is 1. 24 hour urine protein, 2. spot urine protein–creatinine ratio (PCR), 3. spot urine albumin–creatinine ratio (ACR), 4. urine dipstick test. (Book p744)

questions.q: All of the following are listed tests for proteinuria EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Tests: 24 hour urine protein; spot PCR; spot ACR; urine dipstick test. (Book p744)

questions.q: Fill up: The urine dipstick test for protein is described under 'Tests for proteinuria' as a ______ analysis.
questions.exp: Entry 4 reads 'urine dipstick test — qualitative analysis', with the two disadvantages branching from it: positive only around 800 mg and detecting only albumin. (Book p744)

questions.q: The urine dipstick test turns positive only when proteinuria reaches roughly:
questions.exp: Dipstick: qualitative; positive only when there is ↑ proteinuria (~800 mg); detects only albumin. (Book p744)

questions.q: Which statement about the dipstick test for protein is TRUE?
opts: It quantifies protein accurately in mg/day
It is positive at microalbuminuric levels
It detects only albumin and should be supplemented with PCR/ACR/24 hrs urine protein
It detects globulins better than albumin
questions.exp: Dipstick detects only albumin; should be supplemented with PCR/ACR/24 hrs urine protein. (Book p744)

questions.q: The size order of urinary cells written is:
questions.exp: Cell size: RBC < WBC < epithelial cell. (Book p745)

questions.q: On the phase-contrast photo, the arrow-labelled cell larger than the surrounding red cells is a:
questions.exp: The figure labels a large white cell among the monomorphic red cells (RBC < WBC < epithelial cell). (Book p745)

questions.q: Phase contrast microscopy with monomorphic red cells in the figure illustrates the category of:
questions.exp: Phase contrast microscopy with monomorphic red cells corresponds to the urological pattern (vs dysmorphic/acanthocytes). (Book p745)

questions.q: The caption printed beneath the first pair of photographs on this page reads:
opts: Polarized oval fat bodies with maltese cross
Phase contrast microscopy with monomorphic red cells
questions.exp: The caption under the large orange field (with the arrow to a large white cell) is 'Phase contrast microscopy with monomorphic red cells'; the other three captions sit on the remaining figures of the page. (Book p745)

questions.q: Tubular epithelial cells on microscopy are described with:
opts: Clear cytoplasm and round eccentric nucleus
questions.exp: Tubular epithelial cell with nucleus: granular cytoplasm & lobulated nucleus. (Book p745)

questions.q: Oval fat bodies under the polarizing microscope show the:
questions.exp: Polarizing microscope: Maltese cross appearance of oval fat bodies. (Book p745)

questions.q: The same Maltese-cross appearance is attributed in blood to babesiosis.
opts: False — the blood bullet lists oval fat bodies instead
True — and the same bullet list also includes ADPKD under blood
True — 'In blood: Babesiosis' is the first bullet under the polarizing microscope line
False — in blood the Maltese cross marks malaria pigment
questions.exp: Polarizing microscope: maltese cross appearance — In blood: babesiosis; In kidney: Fabry's disease, ADPKD, acute/chronic interstitial nephritis, prerenal azotemia. (Book p745)

questions.q: The Maltese cross in the kidney is associated with all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: In blood: babesiosis; in kidney: Fabry's, ADPKD, acute/chronic interstitial nephritis, prerenal azotemia. (Book p745)

questions.q: The Maltese cross seen in the kidney on polarizing microscopy is listed for all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The 'In kidney' list is Fabry's disease, ADPKD, acute/chronic interstitial nephritis and prerenal azotemia; lipiduria of nephrotic syndrome produces oval fat bodies but is not one of the printed kidney causes on this page. (Book p745)

questions.q: A patient with polycystic kidneys has urine microscopy performed under polarized light and the technologist reports Maltese-cross bodies. Reading this page, the correct interpretation is:
opts: A recognised renal cause of the Maltese cross, alongside Fabry's disease and interstitial nephritis
An artefact, since Maltese crosses appear only in blood
questions.exp: ADPKD is one of the four listed renal causes of a Maltese cross on polarizing microscopy, so the finding fits the underlying cystic disease rather than an artefact or a blood parasite. (Book p745)

questions.q: Fill up: Urinary casts are formed in the ______.
questions.exp: Cast formation: distal convoluted tubule (DCT). (Book p745)

questions.q: Hyaline casts are seen in:
questions.exp: Hyaline cast: normal; kidney disease. (Book p745)

questions.q: In this page's cast table, 'Coarse granular cast' is printed as a row label without its own clinical-association cell.
opts: True — only the hyaline and fine granular rows carry condition cells on this page
False — coarse granular casts are marked 'Kidney disease' in a separate cell
False — the coarse granular row is marked 'Normal'
True — and the same is true of the hyaline cast row
questions.exp: The table on p745 shows a hyaline-cast photo against 'Normal, Kidney disease', then a bare 'Coarse granular cast' label, then the fine granular photo against 'Kidney disease'. (Book p745)

questions.q: Coarse and fine granular casts signify:
questions.exp: Coarse/fine granular casts: kidney disease. (Book p745)

questions.q: Match each finding with its association — 1) Hyaline cast 2) Fine/coarse granular cast 3) Oval fat bodies … A) Maltese cross on polarizing microscopy B) Normal as well as kidney disease C) Kidney disease
questions.exp: Hyaline: normal + kidney disease; granular: kidney disease; oval fat bodies: Maltese cross. (Book p745)

questions.q: Pigment fine granular casts point to pigment nephropathy caused by:
questions.exp: Pigment fine granular cast: pigment nephropathy – hemolysis; rhabdomyolysis. (Book p746)

questions.q: Pigment nephropathy with pigment fine granular casts arises from all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Pigment nephropathy: hemolysis, rhabdomyolysis; nephrotic syndrome instead gives fatty casts/lipiduria. (Book p746)

questions.q: Each cast row on this page is followed by a bullet list of several associations EXCEPT:
opts: RBC cast, whose cell carries one unbulleted line
questions.exp: The RBC cast row shows a single line — 'Glomerular hematuria' — whereas the WBC cast, fatty cast and pigment fine granular rows each carry bulleted lists. (Book p746)

questions.q: Which cast statement is TRUE as per the table?
opts: WBC casts occur in acute pyelonephritis, post-streptococcal GN and ATN/AIN
WBC casts are specific for chronic kidney disease
questions.exp: WBC cast: acute pyelonephritis; PSGN; ATN/AIN. RBC cast = glomerular hematuria; waxy = CKD. (Book p746)

questions.q: Fill up: In the WBC-cast row, the page expands AIN as acute interstitial ______.
questions.exp: The third bullet of that row is printed as 'Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN)/Acute Interstitial Necrosis (AIN)' — the abbreviation is expanded as necrosis on this page even though the cast is classically linked with interstitial nephritis. (Book p746)

questions.q: The cast described as most specific for ATN/AIN is the:
questions.exp: Tubular epithelial cast (muddy brown): ATN/AIN (most specific). (Book p746)

questions.q: Fill up: The muddy brown cast of ATN/AIN is a ______ cast.
questions.exp: Tubular epithelial cast (muddy brown): ATN/AIN (most specific). (Book p746)

questions.q: A post-operative oliguric patient has muddy-brown pigmented casts with renal tubular cells on microscopy. According to this table, that cast is:
opts: A broad cast, which marks chronic kidney disease
A fractured cast, which marks myeloma
The tubular epithelial cast, the most specific marker of ATN/AIN
A pigment fine granular cast, which marks pigment nephropathy
questions.exp: The row reads 'Tubular epithelial cast (muddy brown) — ATN/AIN (most specific)', the phrase in brackets being the page's qualifier for this cast alone. (Book p746)

questions.q: The wording 'ATN/AIN' is written against more than one cast row in this table.
opts: True — and the RBC cast row repeats it for glomerular hematuria
True — the tubular epithelial row adds 'most specific' and the eosinophil row carries the bare pair
False — only the tubular epithelial row mentions it
False — the eosinophil row is instead marked 'myeloma'
questions.exp: ATN/AIN appears in the WBC-cast bullet list, as 'ATN/AIN (most specific)' for the tubular epithelial (muddy brown) cast and again for the eosinophil cast. (Book p746)

questions.q: Broad casts and waxy casts are the markers of:
questions.exp: Broad cast and waxy cast: chronic kidney disease. (Book p746)

questions.q: Which two casts are drawn side by side in a single cell that shares the one association 'Chronic kidney disease'?
opts: Hyaline cast and fine granular cast
questions.exp: The row contains two photographs captioned Broad cast and Waxy cast against a single merged cell reading 'Chronic kidney disease'. (Book p746)

questions.q: Fatty casts are associated with:
questions.exp: Fatty cast: lipiduria (nephrotic syndrome); Fabry's. (Book p746)

questions.q: Match each cast with its association — 1) RBC cast 2) WBC cast 3) Fatty cast … A) Lipiduria (nephrotic syndrome), Fabry's B) Glomerular hematuria C) Acute pyelonephritis, PSGN, ATN/AIN
questions.exp: RBC cast – glomerular hematuria; WBC cast – acute pyelonephritis, PSGN, ATN/AIN; fatty cast – lipiduria, Fabry's. (Book p746)

questions.q: A patient with drug-induced interstitial injury shows casts packed with eosinophils. The association listed is:
questions.exp: Eosinophil cast: ATN/AIN. (Book p746)

questions.q: Fractured casts, seen on biopsy, are associated with:
questions.exp: Fractured cast (on biopsy): myeloma. (Book p746)

questions.q: Match each cast with its association — 1) Broad & waxy casts 2) Fractured cast (on biopsy) 3) Eosinophil cast … A) ATN/AIN B) Myeloma C) Chronic kidney disease
questions.exp: Broad/waxy – CKD; fractured – myeloma; eosinophil – ATN/AIN. (Book p746)

questions.q: Panels A, B and C form the top row of the figure and are captioned uric acid, calcium oxalate dihydrate and calcium oxalate monohydrate in that order.
opts: True — and all three are described as envelope shaped
True — that is the sequence of the three captions
False — panel B is calcium oxalate monohydrate and C is dihydrate
False — panel A is captioned calcium phosphate
questions.exp: Top row: A uric acid (rhomboid), B calcium oxalate dihydrate (bipyramidal/envelope), C calcium oxalate monohydrate (dumb bell). (Book p747)

questions.q: All of the following crystal-shape pairs are as printed EXCEPT:
opts: Calcium oxalate monohydrate - dumb bell shaped
questions.exp: Uric acid crystals are rhomboid; envelope shape belongs to calcium oxalate dihydrate. (Book p747)

questions.q: A stone former's microscopy shows bipyramidal, envelope-shaped crystals. The crystal type is:
questions.exp: Calcium oxalate dihydrate: bipyramidal/envelope shaped. (Book p747)

questions.q: Which crystal statement is TRUE as per the figure labels?
opts: Calcium oxalate monohydrate is envelope shaped while the dihydrate is dumb bell shaped
Calcium oxalate monohydrate is dumb bell shaped while the dihydrate is envelope shaped
questions.exp: Monohydrate – dumb bell; dihydrate – bipyramidal/envelope; cholesterol crystals are listed without those shapes. (Book p747)

questions.q: Star-shaped crystals forming in alkaline urine are:
questions.exp: Calcium phosphate (in alkaline urine): star shaped. (Book p747)

questions.q: The coffin-lid crystal with the formula MgNH4PO4 is:
questions.exp: Struvite (MgNH4PO4): coffin lid appearance. (Book p747)

questions.q: Match each crystal with its shape — 1) Uric acid 2) Calcium oxalate dihydrate 3) Struvite (MgNH4PO4) … A) Coffin lid appearance B) Rhomboid crystals C) Bipyramidal / envelope shaped
questions.exp: Uric acid – rhomboid; calcium oxalate dihydrate – bipyramidal/envelope; struvite – coffin lid. (Book p747)

questions.q: Which panel of this figure page names its crystal but prints no shape descriptor at all?
questions.exp: Panel F is captioned simply 'Cholesterol crystal', while every other caption carries a shape: rhomboid, bipyramidal/envelope, dumb bell, star shaped, coffin lid and hexagonal. (Book p747)

questions.q: Match each figure letter with its printed caption — 1) D 2) E 3) F … A) Cholesterol crystal B) Calcium phosphate (in alkaline urine), star shaped C) Struvite (MgNH4PO4), coffin lid appearance D) Amoxicillin crystal, broom brush appearance
questions.exp: The second row of photographs runs D — calcium phosphate in alkaline urine (star shaped), E — struvite (MgNH4PO4, coffin lid), F — cholesterol; the broom-brush amoxicillin panel sits in the bottom row. (Book p747)

questions.q: The broom brush appearance on urine microscopy belongs to crystals of:
questions.exp: Amoxicillin crystal: broom brush appearance. (Book p747)

questions.q: Fill up: The hexagonal crystals seen on urine microscopy are ______ crystals.
questions.exp: Hexagonal cystine crystal. (Book p747)

questions.q: Match each crystal with its description — 1) Calcium oxalate monohydrate 2) Calcium phosphate 3) Cystine … A) Hexagonal crystal B) Dumb bell shaped C) Star shaped in alkaline urine
questions.exp: Calcium oxalate monohydrate – dumb bell; calcium phosphate – star shaped (alkaline urine); cystine – hexagonal. (Book p747)

questions.q: Every crystal below is paired with the shape descriptor printed under its photograph EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The coffin-lid appearance belongs to struvite; the cholesterol caption carries no shape at all. (Book p747)
